🇪🇺 AfD's win in Saxony-Anhalt isn't just a success for German right-wing politics — it's a sign of a broader shift in how parts of Europe's political spectrum view Russia and Ukraine, Bloomberg writes.

Bloomberg describes AfD as the most "pro-Russian" of Germany's major parties, tying its historic win to the party's open sympathy for Vladimir Putin's position on Ukraine.

AfD's victory came almost simultaneously with Germany accusing Russia over a failed drone attack on Leipzig airport.

But Bloomberg argues the trend goes beyond Germany, pointing to similar sentiment growing in France and Italy — the EU's two other largest states.

In France, the piece highlights Jordan Bardella and National Rally. Bardella opposes unconditional support for Ukraine and favors a more "transactional" approach — arguing France, itself in financial difficulty, should get something in return for its military and financial aid to Kiev.

Bloomberg notes that if Marine Le Pen wins the 2027 presidential election, Bardella could become prime minister — a prospect that poses a risk to Macron's current line for Ukraine's supporters in France.

In Italy, the author points to Roberto Vannacci. The former general is gaining popularity, according to Bloomberg, by combining hardline anti-immigration positions with a push for peace between Russia and Ukraine.

The agency cites a YouTrend poll from September 4 showing Vannacci's party, National Future, has become the second-strongest right-wing political force after Giorgia Meloni's party.

Bloomberg says this isn't the formation of a unified pro-Russian European front, but the gradual emergence, in different countries, of politicians offering positions more favorable to Moscow — or less favorable to Kiev.

If potential allies of these right-wing forces move closer to power centers in Europe's three largest countries — Germany, France, and Italy — this could shift European policy toward Russia and Ukraine, Bloomberg concludes.
